name: Back Lever
summary: Face-down horizontal lever from German hang. Rings preferred. Do not skip tissue conditioning.

programming.notes: Lower frequency than FL due to biceps/shoulder tissue risk.

safety.notes: Rings strongly preferred. Stop immediately on biceps/shoulder pain. Earn German hang 30–45s before any lever work.

divergence_notes: Some coaches teach BL before FL (easier for many); this tree follows tissue-readiness (German hang first).

timeline.from_level: 30s pain-free German hang, 5 controlled skin the cats, 8 strict pull-ups
timeline.human_label: 10 months – 2 years from a comfortable German hang; the full back lever itself typically lands at 8–18 months
timeline.notes: Consistently reported as arriving earlier than the front lever, with biceps-tendon tolerance and shoulder-extension mobility — not pulling strength — as the rate limiters. The tissue steps at the start of this tree are deliberately slow; every week skipped there tends to reappear as a forced layoff later.

variance_drivers.note: Straight-arm and pulling skills scale roughly with bodyweight at a fixed height. Athletes above ~85 kg routinely sit at the top of every band; lighter athletes at the bottom. This is the single largest driver on lever and planche trees.

Rate of adaptation is logarithmic. An athlete with 3+ years of consistent resistance training moves through early steps in a fraction of the listed time but gains little advantage on the last two steps of any tree.
Connective tissue remodels more slowly with age. Athletes over ~40 should read the upper half of every band and extend tendon-conditioning steps rather than compressing them.
Longer arms and legs lengthen the lever at a fixed bodyweight. Taller athletes commonly need one extra intermediate shape (one-leg before straddle) that shorter athletes can skip.
Below roughly 2 quality sessions per week most athletes stall indefinitely on advanced steps. Gains from going beyond 4–5 sessions per week are small and injury risk rises (arampatzis-2024-loading).
Video review or a coach correcting shape is repeatedly reported to roughly halve time-to-skill on balance-dominant work versus unguided practice (kyleweiger-handstand).

prerequisite_standards.name: German hang
prerequisite_standards.rationale: Non-negotiable. Every back-lever injury story starts with skipping this.

prerequisite_standards.name: Skin the cat
prerequisite_standards.rationale: Controlled entry and exit from the bottom position.

prerequisite_standards.name: Tuck front lever
prerequisite_standards.rationale: Balances the straight-arm pull in both directions and reduces the shoulder-load asymmetry.

plateau_signatures.signal: Strength feels available but the biceps or front of the shoulder complains before the set ends
typical_causes: Progressing on lever length faster than tissue can adapt
resolution: Return to German hang volume for 4–8 weeks
Add light supine bar hangs as dedicated tendon conditioning
Hold the current lever longer rather than lengthening it

plateau_signatures.signal: The hold looks long but the body settles below parallel
typical_causes: Chasing hold time instead of position
Using the passive end-range as a rest position, which loads the tendon rather than the muscle
resolution: Film every attempt and score only the time spent at or above horizontal
Shorten the target and rebuild strictly

regression_triggers.trigger: Layoff or markedly reduced training for less than 4 weeks (illness, travel, work crunch)
regression_triggers.typical_dropback: No step lost. Hold times commonly return 10–25% short for the first two sessions; eccentric control and shape quality degrade before maximal strength does.
regression_triggers.action: Resume one step below your unlock for two sessions, then retest. Do not re-earn the whole step — strength-trained athletes show only limited decline at this timescale.

regression_triggers.typical_dropback: Force production falls roughly 7–12%, which usually costs one step on hold-based progressions and one to two steps on the hardest dynamic ones. Recently acquired gains are retained far better than the loss in maximal force suggests.
regression_triggers.action: Restart two steps below your previous unlock and rebuild with full volume but reduced intensity. Expect to regain the lost steps in a fraction of the time they originally took.

regression_triggers.trigger: Planned deload, or four consecutive weeks with no measurable progress
regression_triggers.typical_dropback: None. Hold times often improve in the week after the deload.
regression_triggers.action: Cut volume roughly in half and keep intensity, for one week. Overcoming Gravity's rule is that four weeks without progress means the cycle is finished, not that you need to try harder.

regression_triggers.trigger: Tendon pain forcing modified or stopped training
regression_triggers.typical_dropback: Highly variable. Time lost is usually 6–12 weeks because the tissue must be reloaded from a low baseline, and the affected step is typically lost entirely.
regression_triggers.action: Drop to the last pain-free step, reintroduce isometric then slow eccentric loading, and rebuild across at least 8–12 weeks — the window in which tendon stiffness actually changes. Returning at the previous intensity is the most common cause of recurrence.

injury_risk_timeline.mechanism: Peak long-head biceps tension: straight elbow, extended shoulder, and a lengthening lever. Risk climbs with every shape change because the moment arm grows faster than tissue adapts.
prophylaxis: Accumulate 8+ weeks of German hang before any lever shape
Add one shape change at a time and hold it for at least 4 weeks
Keep light supine hangs in the programme permanently
Use rings so the forearms can rotate
red_flags: Pain on resisted elbow flexion the day after
A sensation of 'giving way' at the front of the shoulder

injury_risk_timeline.mechanism: Straight-arm loading at the longest lever, with dynamic entry adding a velocity spike
prophylaxis: Never enter the lever by dropping into it
Keep dynamic raises to low reps and high quality

productive.notes: Deliberately lower than the portfolio default. This tree is limited by connective-tissue tolerance rather than by muscular recovery, and tissue does not care how motivated you are.

too_much_signals: Needing a longer German hang warm-up each week to feel ready
Hold times falling while perceived effort rises

deload.protocol: One week of German hang and tuck holds only, at half the usual sets.
deload.trigger: Any tendon symptom, or four weeks without progress.
